title: Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI)
path: Management of Clients with Musculoskeletal Problems

headings.title: Introduction and Core Principles of MRI
headings.content: Magnetic Resonance Imaging is a diagnostic modality that utilizes powerful magnetic fields and radiofrequency waves to generate detailed cross-sectional images of internal body structures. Unlike X-rays or computed tomography scans, this technology avoids ionizing radiation entirely. Hydrogen atoms, abundant within the body's water and fat molecules, serve as the primary focus during the scan. When exposed to the scanner's strong magnetic field, these protons align. Radiofrequency pulses then temporarily knock them out of alignment. As the protons return to their resting state, they emit signals that specialized computer algorithms translate into high-contrast anatomical images.

headings.title: Safety Protocols and Contraindications
headings.content:
The intense magnetic field of the scanner remains active constantly, transforming any ferromagnetic object into a high-speed projectile. Safety screening must be rigorous prior to entering the scan room. 

- **Absolute Contraindications**: Cardiac pacemakers, implantable cardioverter-defibrillators, cochlear implants, and certain intracranial aneurysm clips.
- **Relative Contraindications**: Pregnancy during the first trimester, severe claustrophobia, metallic foreign bodies in the eye, and non-removable medical infusion pumps.
- **Transmissible Hazards**: Oxygen cylinders, surgical instruments, and stethoscopes brought near the aperture can cause catastrophic equipment damage or patient injury.

headings.title: Pre-Procedure Preparation and Assessment
headings.content: Comprehensive preparation minimizes patient anxiety and prevents adverse events inside the scanning suite. The nursing staff must conduct a thorough screening interview to identify implanted metals, tattoos containing metallic ink, and renal function status if contrast media is ordered. Patients should change into a hospital gown to eliminate hidden fasteners or metallic threads. All jewelry, hearing aids, dentures, and watches must be removed and securely stored. Providing clear explanations regarding the loud, repetitive knocking noises helps mitigate claustrophobia and reduces movement artifacts.

headings.title: Intra-Procedure Care and Monitoring
headings.content: During image acquisition, the client must remain completely still on the narrow examination table. Even minor movements blur the digital matrix and necessitate repeating sequences. Staff monitor the client via a specialized observation window, intercom system, and physiological monitoring equipment compatible with the magnetic environment. Earplugs or acoustic headphones are mandatory to protect hearing against the loud acoustic noise produced by gradient coils switching rapidly on and off. A call bell or squeeze ball is placed in the client's hand to signal staff if distress arises.

headings.title: Post-Procedure Management and Complications
headings.content: Following the completion of imaging sequences, care shifts to monitoring recovery, particularly if sedation or contrast was utilized. If gadolinium contrast was administered, nurses observe the insertion site for localized extravasation and monitor for rare hypersensitivity reactions such as hives or respiratory distress. Clients who received oral or intravenous sedatives require close observation in a recovery area until vital signs stabilize and orientation returns to baseline. Normal activities and diet can typically resume immediately unless specific sedation restrictions apply.
